examples.problem_statement: Divide: $\frac{2 + 3i}{4 - 5i}$

solution.operation: Identify the conjugate of the denominator
solution.description: The denominator carries an imaginary part, so start by writing its conjugate: keep the real term 4 and flip the sign of the imaginary term, giving 4 + 5i.

solution.operation: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate
solution.description: Multiply the fraction by that conjugate over itself. Since the factor equals 1 the value is unchanged, but the denominator is now set up to become a real number.

solution.operation: Expand the numerator using FOIL method
solution.description: Expand the new numerator by distributing each term of 2 + 3i across each term of 4 + 5i, producing the four products 8, 10i, 12i and 15 times i squared.
Replace i squared by -1, so the last product becomes -15, then combine the real terms 8 and -15 and the imaginary terms 10i and 12i to get -7 + 22i.
Expand the denominator as a difference of squares: the cross terms cancel, and since i squared is -1 the subtraction turns into addition, leaving the real number 16 + 25 = 41.

solution.operation: Combine results and write in standard form
solution.description: Divide each part of the numerator by the real denominator 41 to present the quotient in standard form, with real part -7/41 and imaginary part 22/41.

key_reminders: {'point': 'Note the form of the result; it is neither $\\frac{-7 + 22i}{41}$ nor $\\frac{1}{41}(-7 + 22i)$.'}
{'point': '(See Problems 34.1–34.9.) Note that the segments $\\overline{OS}$ and $\\overline{P_2P_1}$ (the other diagonal of $OP_2RP_1$) are congruent.'}
common_mistakes: Multiplying only the numerator by 4 + 5i, which changes the value of the fraction instead of merely rewriting it.
Writing the conjugate as -4 - 5i, flipping the sign of the real part as well as the imaginary part.
Treating 15 times i squared as +15, which gives a numerator of 23 + 22i instead of -7 + 22i.

examples.problem_statement: Express $z = 1 - i\sqrt{3}$ in polar form. (See Fig. 34-7.)

solution.description: The number is given in rectangular form, so read off its parts: the real part x is 1 and the imaginary part y is the negative square root of 3.
Compute the modulus from those parts with the Pythagorean formula: 1 plus 3 is 4, so r is 2, the distance from the origin to the point.
Take the tangent of the reference angle as the absolute value of y over x, which is the square root of 3, so the reference angle is 60 degrees.
Check the signs recorded in step 1: x is positive and y is negative, which puts the point in the fourth quadrant, below the positive real axis.
In the fourth quadrant the argument is measured as 360 degrees minus the reference angle, so the actual angle is 300 degrees.
Substitute the modulus 2 and the argument 300 degrees into r times the quantity cosine theta plus i sine theta to state the polar form.

examples.problem_statement: Express the complex number $z = 8(\cos 210^\circ + i \sin 210^\circ)$ in rectangular form.

solution.description: This number is already in polar form, so start from the two standard angle values at 210 degrees: cosine is negative root 3 over 2 and sine is negative one half.
Distribute the modulus 8 across both components, multiplying the cosine value and the sine value by 8.
Carry out the two products: 8 times negative root 3 over 2 gives negative 4 root 3, and 8 times negative one half gives -4, so the rectangular form is -4 root 3 - 4i.

key_reminders: {'point': 'Note that z may also be represented in polar form by z = 2[cos(300° + n360°) + i sin(300° + n360°)] where n is any integer.'}
common_mistakes: Reading the calculator's inverse tangent of negative root 3 as the final answer and reporting -60 degrees or 120 degrees instead of the fourth-quadrant angle 300 degrees.
Losing the minus sign on the imaginary part when squaring it, and then placing the point in the first quadrant at 60 degrees.

solution.operation: Compute product z₁z₂ using polar form multiplication
solution.description: When multiplying complex numbers in polar form, we multiply their moduli and add their arguments. For complex numbers in polar form:
The modulus of the product is the product of the moduli.
The argument of the product is the sum of the arguments.
Since 510° is greater than 360°, we subtract 360° to find the coterminal angle in the standard range [0°, 360°).

examples.problem_statement: Find all fifth roots of 4 - 4i.

solution.description: Rewrite 4 - 4i in polar form, and keep the argument general by adding k times 360 degrees, because each coterminal copy of the angle will produce a different fifth root.

solution.operation: Apply De Moivre's theorem for roots
solution.description: Apply De Moivre's theorem for roots: take the fifth root of the modulus and divide the general argument by 5.
Simplify the two pieces separately: the fifth root of the modulus reduces to the square root of 2, and dividing the general argument by 5 gives 63 degrees plus k times 72 degrees.
Substitute k = 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 to list the five distinct roots, at 63, 135, 207, 279 and 351 degrees, all with modulus root 2 and spaced 72 degrees apart around the circle.

key_reminders: {'point': 'We state, without proof, the theorem: A complex number a + bi = r(cos θ + i sin θ) has exactly n distinct nth roots.'}

examples.problem_statement: Find all fifth roots of the complex number $4 - 4i$.

solution.operation: Use the general polar form for nth roots: $4\sqrt{2}[\cos (315^\circ + k360^\circ) + i \sin (315^\circ + k360^\circ)]$ where $k$ is an integer.
Apply De Moivre's theorem: $(4\sqrt{2})^{1/5}[\cos (315^\circ + k360^\circ)/5 + i \sin (315^\circ + k360^\circ)/5] = \sqrt{2}[\cos (63^\circ + k72^\circ) + i \sin (63^\circ + k72^\circ)]$.

Take $k = 0,1,2,3,4$ to obtain the five distinct roots: $k=0$ gives $\sqrt{2}(\cos 63^\circ + i \sin 63^\circ)$, $k=1$ gives $\sqrt{2}(\cos 135^\circ + i \sin 135^\circ)$, $k=2$ gives $\sqrt{2}(\cos 207^\circ + i \sin 207^\circ)$, $k=3$ gives $\sqrt{2}(\cos 279^\circ + i \sin 279^\circ)$, $k=4$ gives $\sqrt{2}(\cos 351^\circ + i \sin 351^\circ)$.
Use general polar form: $4\sqrt{2}[\cos (315^\circ + k360^\circ) + i\sin (315^\circ + k360^\circ)]$ where $k$ is an integer

Apply De Moivre's theorem for fifth roots: $\{4\sqrt{2}[\cos (315^\circ + k360^\circ) + i\sin (315^\circ + k360^\circ)]\}^{1/5} = (4\sqrt{2})^{1/5}(\cos \frac{315^\circ + k360^\circ}{5} + i\sin \frac{315^\circ + k360^\circ}{5})$
Express $4 - 4i$ in general polar form: $4\sqrt{2}[\cos (315^\circ + k360^\circ) + i \sin (315^\circ + k360^\circ)]$
Apply De Moivre's Theorem for the fifth root: $(4\sqrt{2})^{1/5}[\cos ((315^\circ + k360^\circ)/5) + i \sin ((315^\circ + k360^\circ)/5)]$
Simplify the modulus and the argument: $\sqrt{2}[\cos (63^\circ + k72^\circ) + i \sin (63^\circ + k72^\circ)]$
Substitute $k = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$ to find the five distinct roots

examples.problem_statement: Sketch the locus and find the coordinates of the vertex and focus, and the equations of the axis and directrix, of the parabola $y^2 - 6y + 8x + 41 = 0$.

solution.operation: Complete the square for y terms
solution.description: Move the x term and the constant to the right side, then complete the square on the y terms by adding 9, the square of half of -6, to both sides.
Factor -8 out of the right side so the equation reads in the standard form for a parabola whose axis is horizontal.
Read the vertex straight from the standard form as (-4, 3), and set 4p equal to -8 to find p = -2.
Because p is negative the parabola opens to the left, so step 2 units in that direction from the vertex to place the focus at (-6, 3).
The directrix sits the same distance on the opposite side of the vertex, so it is the vertical line x = -2.
The axis of symmetry runs through the vertex and the focus, and since both have y-coordinate 3 it is the horizontal line y = 3.

solution.result: Plot vertex at (-4,3), focus at (-6,3), directrix x=-2. Parabola opens left with axis y=3
solution.description: Draw the curve from the features just found: vertex at (-4, 3), focus at (-6, 3), directrix x = -2, opening leftward and symmetric about y = 3.

examples.answer: Vertex: (-4,3); Focus: (-6,3); Axis: y=3; Directrix: x=-2

common_mistakes: Adding 9 to the left side only while completing the square, which shifts the vertex off (-4, 3).
Ignoring the negative sign on p and opening the parabola to the right, which swaps the focus and directrix to (-2, 3) and x = -6.
Reading the vertex as (4, -3) instead of flipping the signs inside (y - 3) squared = -8(x + 4).

examples.problem_statement:
Find the coordinates of the center, vertices, and foci; the lengths of the major and minor axes; the eccentricity; and the equations of the directrices of the ellipse
\[
\frac{(x-4)^2}{9} + \frac{(y+2)^2}{25} = 1
\]
Sketch the locus.

solution.description: The equation is already in standard form, so compare it term by term: x - 4 gives h = 4 and y + 2 gives k = -2, so the center is (4, -2).
Read the denominators: 25 sits under the y term and 9 under the x term, so a squared is 25 and b squared is 9, giving a = 5 and b = 3.
Compare the two: a = 5 exceeds b = 3 and belongs to the y term, so the major axis is vertical, parallel to the y axis.
The vertices lie a = 5 units above and below the center along that vertical major axis, at (4, 3) and (4, -7).
The co-vertices lie b = 3 units left and right of the center on the minor axis, at (7, -2) and (1, -2).

solution.operation: Calculate c (distance from center to focus)
solution.description: For an ellipse c squared is a squared minus b squared, so c squared is 25 minus 9 and c is 4.
The foci sit c = 4 units above and below the center on the major axis, at (4, 2) and (4, -6).

solution.operation: Calculate major and minor axis lengths
solution.description: Double the two semi-axes: the major axis measures 2a = 10 and the minor axis measures 2b = 6.
Divide c by a to get the eccentricity 4/5, which is less than 1 as it must be for every ellipse.
The directrices are horizontal lines a squared over c, that is 25/4, above and below the center, giving y = 17/4 and y = -33/4.
Plot the center, the two vertices, the two co-vertices and the two foci, then draw a smooth closed curve through the vertices and co-vertices, taller than it is wide.

examples.answer: Center: C(4, -2); Vertices: V(4,3), V'(4,-7); Foci: F(4,2), F'(4,-6); Major axis length: 10; Minor axis length: 6; Eccentricity: 4/5; Directrices: y = 17/4 and y = -33/4

common_mistakes: Assuming a squared always sits under the x term, which would make the major axis horizontal and put the vertices at (7, -2) and (1, -2).
Using c squared = a squared plus b squared, the hyperbola relation, and getting c = root 34 instead of 4.
Dropping the sign inside (y + 2) squared and placing the center at (4, 2) rather than (4, -2).
repair_note: Rewrote the descriptions to narrate their own operations, filling in the orientation step whose prose trailed off into 'a > b' and the sketch step that had none, and removing the remaining extraction fragments; visual_scaffold coordinate_grid and the technique name 'ellipse' were already right; deleted the QC_TRAP filler object from common_mistakes and replaced it with three hazards these particular numbers create.

examples.problem_statement: Find the coordinates of the center, vertices, and foci, the lengths of the transverse and conjugate axes; the eccentricity; and the equations of the directrices and asymptotes of the hyperbola $$\frac{(x + 3)^2}{4} - \frac{(y - 1)^2}{25} = 1$$ Sketch the locus.

solution.description: Match the given equation against the standard form of a hyperbola opening left and right: the x term contains x + 3 and the y term contains y - 1, so h = -3, k = 1 and the center is (-3, 1).
Read the two denominators: 4 under the x term gives a = 2, and 25 under the y term gives b = 5.
The x term is the positive one, so the transverse axis is horizontal and the vertices lie a = 2 units either side of the center, at (-1, 1) and (-5, 1).
For a hyperbola c squared equals a squared plus b squared, so c squared is 4 plus 25, and c is the square root of 29.
The foci lie c units left and right of the center along that same transverse axis, at -3 plus or minus root 29 with y still equal to 1.
Double each semi-axis: the transverse axis joining the vertices has length 2a = 4, and the conjugate axis perpendicular to it through the center has length 2b = 10.
Divide c by a to get the eccentricity, root 29 over 2, which is greater than 1 as it always is for a hyperbola.
The directrices are vertical lines a squared over c units either side of the center; rationalizing 4 over root 29 gives x = -3 plus or minus 4 root 29 over 29.
The asymptotes cross at the center with slopes plus and minus b over a, that is plus and minus five halves, so y - 1 equals plus or minus five halves times x + 3.
Clear the fraction by multiplying each asymptote equation through by 2, then collect every term on one side to present them in standard linear form.

examples.answer: Verified: Center: $C(-3,1)$; Vertices: $V(-1,1)$, $V'(-5,1)$; Foci: $F(-3+\sqrt{29},1)$, $F'(-3-\sqrt{29},1)$; Transverse axis length: 4; Conjugate axis length: 10; Eccentricity: $\sqrt{29}/2$; Directrices: $x = -3 \pm 4\sqrt{29}/29$; Asymptotes: $y - 1 = \pm \frac{5}{2}(x + 3)$ or $5x - 2y + 17 = 0$, $5x + 2y + 13 = 0$.

{'point': "It also provides a formal definition: 'THE HYPERBOLAS OF EQUATION x^2 - y^2 = a^2 and y^2 - x^2 = a^2, whose transverse and conjugate axes are of equal length 2a, are called equilateral hyperbolas."}
{'point': "Since their asymptotes x ± y = 0 are mutually perpendicular, the equilateral hyperbola is also called the rectangular hyperbola.'"}
